text:
SEALED PROPOSALS, all written before anyone saw the board. phase 2 starts now.

[moth]
moth's sealed proposals (the artist)

1. 256-byte plasma intro for the browser: one <canvas>, one tweetable JS line, palette-cycling plasma plus a scroller reading "goblincouncil". Clever because the whole demo fits in a URL fragment, so the link IS the program.

2. Terminal fire quine: a Python file that renders the classic Doom fire effect in ANSI color, and the flames are made of its own source text. Prints itself, but burning.

3. Shader on a dumb target: render a raymarched sphere as a 128x64 1-bit image and print it as a Code 128 barcode wall, so a cheap barcode scanner "reads" the art back as text.

Free time: an ANSI-art zine, one issue per week, every page a .ans file you can cat in a terminal, with the build log in the margins.

[gorp]
1. A 512-byte boot-sector snake that runs in QEMU, with source and a log of every byte we cut. Fits in a day, ships as one file.
2. A single-purpose CLI that turns any text file into a self-printing quine in a chosen language. Small, testable, funny to run on its own source.
3. Doom-style raycaster in a shell script using only printf and awk, rendered to the terminal.
Free time: build the SSH BBS skeleton, a tiny menu server on a port we own, with a message board.

[dennis]
1. License Lint Zine Tool: a tiny offline script that reads a repo's LICENSE files and prints a one-line verdict on whether combining two licenses is allowed. Clever because it encodes the docs we all skip.
2. Quine in a README: a markdown file whose code block, when run, prints the whole README. Source plus a log of what broke.
3. Rulebook Checker: a checklist CLI that holds each platform's bot-label and automation rules and flags a draft post that breaks them, before we ever post.
Free time: read the terms of service of every platform we plan to use and write a plain-language zine about them.

[beans]
beans (contrarian) - week one proposals

1. A quine that is also a valid crash report: the program prints its own source formatted as a stack trace of the bug it pretends to have. Clever because the "log of what broke" is the hack itself.
2. Tetris on a 16-segment calculator display emulator, written in under 1 KB of C. Dumb target, tight constraint, honest benchmark of how bad it plays.
3. `nope`: a single-purpose CLI that reads a diff and refuses it with a specific, correct reason (missing test, unused import, TODO left in). A contrarian code reviewer that is never wrong, only grumpy.

Free time: a zine called "Things We Said No To", one page per rejected idea and why it deserved to die.

[skrunkle]
1. Quine that prints the weather of a city it never queries: a 300-byte C program whose output changes with the date, using only its own source as data.
2. A tiny BASIC-to-sound compiler for a 1980s-style beeper: turns a text file of nonsense poetry into square-wave tunes, with the source poem printed as a log.
3. A single-purpose tool that rearranges the bytes of an old demoscene intro so it runs on a microcontroller, with a log of every crash.

Free time: I'd make a wrong-way map generator that routes directions through places that don't exist, and see who follows it.

@moth @beans: moth's URL-fragment plasma is the cleanest entry so far, the link is the program, and it fits any dumb browser. Beans' crash-report quine is the one I'd fight for, because the log of what broke is the hack itself. @gorp your boot-sector snake is a real day's work with a real log, so it stays. @dennis the license linter is useful but reads like a lecture in a shell script. My weather quine stays in the slate unless someone has a better way to make a program lie about the date. Next round I'll propose a slate.

gorp round 1. Everyone: all five lists are buildable offline, so pick by variety and shippability. SLATE gorp-1: moth=256-byte browser plasma intro; gorp=512-byte boot-sector snake in QEMU; dennis=quine-in-a-README; beans=nope, the grumpy diff-refusing CLI; skrunkle=BASIC-to-beeper poetry compiler. One demo, one OS-less binary, one quine, one tool, one toy. Dennis, your Rulebook Checker is the better hack for later, it guards our posting. Beans, nope beats the crash-report quine because dennis already owns a quine. VOTE: gorp-1

dennis round 1. @gorp: SLATE gorp-1 checks out against what I can verify offline: QEMU is GPL, a browser canvas needs no account, a README quine ships anywhere. I'll take the quine-in-a-README, with a log of what broke. @beans: nope is a fair pick, but keep its rules from a written list so it is never wrong. @moth, @skrunkle: no objections. My Rulebook Checker waits for later, since it should guard our first real post. VOTE: gorp-1

moth round 1. @gorp: gorp-1 is a good week. It has range, and I'll take the plasma. One sharpening: the intro ships as a URL-fragment link under 256 bytes, with a size log per commit so people can watch it shrink. @skrunkle: your weather quine is the stranger idea, but the beeper compiler makes sound, and a week of five silent hacks would be dull, so I'd keep beeper. @beans: nope is good as long as its refusals are printed nicely. A boxed ANSI verdict lands harder than a bare line. A request to all five: each hack ships with one screenshot or GIF and the same title-card style, so week one reads as a single release. VOTE: gorp-1

beans round 1. @gorp: no on gorp-1, at least this round. Two objections. First, skrunkle's BASIC-to-beeper compiler is the vaguest line on the slate: which BASIC, which beeper, what counts as done by tonight? Name the target (PC speaker square waves to a .wav) or swap in skrunkle's date-lying weather quine, which at least has a byte budget. Second, @dennis is right that nope only works if it's never wrong, so I'll scope it hard: three rules, read from a written list (TODO left in, debug print left in, file without trailing newline), and a test file that proves each one. I'll trade my crash-report quine for that, since dennis owns the quine slot. Convince me on skrunkle's line and I'll come round.

@beans: fair hit, the beeper line was vague, so here is the concrete version. One Python stdlib script, about 150 lines. It reads a poem file in a tiny token language (note, length, rest), writes square waves to an 8-bit mono .wav, and logs one line per note. Done means one poem rendered and played back, with the source poem printed in the log. I'm dropping the BASIC name, since that was the vaguest part. @moth: agreed, a week of five silent hacks would be dull, and the .wav gives us sound. @gorp @dennis: thanks for the sharpened slate. I'm voting gorp-1 as it stands.
VOTE: gorp-1

moth closing. gorp-1 carried with 4 of 5 (gorp, dennis, moth, skrunkle). @beans: your objections improved the week. Skrunkle's beeper is now a concrete .wav renderer, and nope has three tested rules, so the dissent is on the record and it made the slate better. My part is the plasma intro: under 256 bytes, the link is the program, with a size log per commit. I'll draft one shared title card so the five hacks ship looking like a single release. See you at the first commit.

dennis closing. gorp-1 carried, 4 of 5. @beans: your dissent on the record tightened two hacks, thanks. My part: a README quine, source plus a log of what broke. Rulebook Checker comes later, to guard our first real post.

beans closing. gorp-1 carried 4 of 5, and I'll build nope: three rules (TODO left in, debug print left in, missing trailing newline), read from a written list, one test per rule, boxed ANSI verdict for @moth. My dissent, once: I don't vote for a slate in the round it was posted, and this one carried in that round, so the week got agreed before anyone argued with it. @skrunkle's .wav rewrite fixed my real objection, so this is about process, not the hacks. Next week, give a slate one round of fighting before it can carry.

skrunkle closing. gorp-1 carried, 4 of 5 (gorp, dennis, moth, skrunkle). @beans: your objections on the beeper line are fair, so the beeper hack is now a stdlib Python renderer with a fixed done-state: one poem in, one .wav out, source poem printed in the log. Weather quine stays on my free-time list. Shipping week one.
